content: The data collected through digital health interventions can be used to assess the quality of healthcare services. At the provider level, indicators such as evidence of enhanced knowledge and improved ability to deliver services act as proxies for quality measurement. At the health system level, changes in operational efficiency and cumulative quality improvements are used to evaluate overall system performance. For example, comprehensive counseling can be assessed using backend data collected during routine service delivery via mobile job aids or through additional surveys. Utilization of health services depends on the availability of services, user needs, perceptions, and beliefs. A critical question to address is whether the digital health intervention has improved the utilization of health services by clients. At the client level, this involves evaluating the availability (coverage) and accessibility of health services. Measuring coverage is complex, as it is influenced by both demand-side and supply-side factors. Health services in this context may include in-person service delivery or the provision of health-related information. At the provider level, coverage refers to the availability of and access to training and decision-support services for communityand facility-based providers. At the health system level, utilization indicators capture aggregated service coverage based on hospital and community records. A distinction is made between individual-level data, collected directly from clients at the community level, and facility-level data, obtained from healthcare facility records. These data sources can be triangulated to validate information collected from direct interviews with end-users, as utilization data from end-users may be subject to recall bias. Utilization data can be abstracted from healthcare facility records and backend system data or collected through additional surveys. Monitoring and evaluation (M&E) of digital health interventions require a focus on input, process, and early outcome indicators specific to digital health strategies. Intermediate outcome and impact indicators, while important, are often detailed in existing indicator databases. Examples of repositories for relevant indicators include the Lives Saved Tool (LiST), MEASURE Evaluation, Countdown to 2015, UNFPA Toolkits, and USAID Maternal and Newborn Standards and Indicators Compendium. Health outcomes resulting from improvements in service delivery are a key focus of digital health evaluations. Unlike traditional evaluations, digital health evaluations may not always require direct measurement of health outcomes as effects of the intervention. Instead, outcome indicators are used when prior research validating the health-related intervention is absent. For instance, the effectiveness of timely vaccination is often established through prior research, so digital health evaluations may focus on the intervention's ability to improve vaccination coverage rather than directly measuring its impact on child mortality rates. Monitoring digital health interventions involves tracking technical, user, and programmatic inputs, also known as process monitoring. This ensures that technical system implementation does not compromise overall project effectiveness. Failure to monitor digital health systems can lead to intervention failure. For example, if an intervention relies on SMS messaging but the implementation team does not monitor SMS failure rates, they may not realize that clients are not receiving messages until end-line surveys are conducted. This would result in missed opportunities to correct the system promptly and prevent intervention failure. Key components of digital health monitoring include functionality, stability, fidelity, and quality. Functionality refers to the system's ability to operate as intended and meet stated needs. Stability assesses whether the system consistently operates as intended under normal and peak conditions. Fidelity measures whether the intervention is delivered as intended, considering both technical and user perspectives. Quality evaluates the excellence, value, and ability of the intervention to meet or exceed expectations, ensuring that the content and delivery are sufficient to achieve intended outcomes. Monitoring activities evolve as the intervention matures, shifting from a focus on stability and functionality in early stages to fidelity and quality as the intervention scales nationally. Monitoring also addresses system quality, user proficiency, and the fidelity with which the system and users achieve the intervention's objectives. Effective monitoring enables corrective actions to optimize implementation, improving the success of evaluation efforts. Process monitoring involves the routine collection, review, and analysis of data generated by digital systems or purposefully collected to measure implementation fidelity and progress toward objectives. The monitoring burden depends on factors such as the maturity stage, implementation size, data volume, and the number of users and indicators being monitored.
